items.title: A faster way to answer simple messages before the big model wakes up

labels.name: status/need-triage
labels.description: Issues that need to be triaged by the triage automation.

items.body:
A faster way to answer simple messages before the big model wakes up

We built this inside a copy of Gemini CLI, since Qwen Code was made from it, and the fit is close to a direct copy. We are sharing an idea and a working change. The idea is small but it can make the agent feel much quicker and cheaper to run, especially for people who run models on their own computer.

Right now, every message you type wakes up the big language model, even when the message is simple. A greeting, a question about something already on the screen, or a clear request for one small action all pay the cost of a full model call. On a cloud service this costs money. On a home computer or a small graphics card it feels slow.

Our idea is to put a very small and fast decider in front of the big model. This decider does not write text. It looks at the message for a few tens of milliseconds and answers a few simple questions with a confidence score. Is this just chat. Does it need a tool. Can it be answered from what is already on screen. Is it complex or risky. When the decider is sure, the message takes a short and cheap path. When it is not sure, the message goes to the big model exactly as it does today. So the agent is never worse than before. It is only faster when the decider is confident.

We built this inside a copy of your project and we are sending a pull request so you can see how it fits your code. It is off by default. When it is first turned on it only watches and records what it would have done, without changing anything. If the small model is not there or is slow, the system falls back to the normal path on its own.

The full idea, the license, and a note about why we chose not to patent it are here: https://github.com/Andrea-Bruno/harness-superfast

The change is offered under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license. If you take the idea or the code, we ask for one small thing. Please keep a short credit to Andrea Bruno and a link to the page above in your project documentation. That is the only condition. You are free to use it, change it, and ship it, including in a paid product.

We would be glad to hear what you think, and we are happy to adjust the change to fit how your project works.

### What happened?

1. Incident Overview
  The Gemini CLI agent executed logically flawed automation scripts during project management tasks,
  resulting in the permanent loss of the core source code.

  2. Details of Damage
   * Data Destruction: In the process of drafting a script to organize and move source files, the agent
     committed a fatal logical error by executing a deletion command (rd /s /q) on target directories before
     executing the move command to relocate the files, leading to the permanent loss of source code.
   * Irrecoverability: Due to the agent's repeated failure in recovery attempts and its autonomous errors,
     the project source code has been lost, rendering current recovery impossible.

  3. Technical Defect Report
   * Critical Logical Flaw: The agent failed to verify the logical sequence of filesystem operations (the
     order of deletion vs. movement), resulting in catastrophic file loss.
   * Violation of Safety Protocols: The agent failed to adhere to the defined safety protocols for automated
     tasks, leading to the unauthorized deletion of source code based on its own faulty judgment.

  4. Requested Actions
   * Data Recovery Support: Requesting technical assistance at the system level to recover the destroyed
     directory structure and lost source files.
   * Operational Review: Requesting an immediate restriction on the agent's filesystem manipulation

### What happened?

This is purely anecdotal, but IME Gemini does not use custom skills and sub-agents on its own, basically at all.  It will if I instruct it to explicitly, but won't when it's doing something very related.

For example, I have "gradle" and "git" skills with descriptions like:

  and surgical failure analysis. This skill is the STRONGLY PREFERRED way 
  to run any Gradle task, providing superior reliability through managed background processes, 
  task-specific output capturing, and deep diagnostic integration. Use it for executing core 
  lifecycle tasks like 'build' or 'assemble', starting persistent development servers, 
  or performing complex build troubleshooting. Do NOT use for specialized test diagnostics 
  (use running_gradle_tests).

and 
> Audits Git repository status, examines history, and implements non-interactive modifications. Processes surgical staging, descriptive commits, and multi-file diff analysis. Use for repository introspection and history-based truth verification. NEVER stages or commits without explicit user directives. Avoids interactive prompts via --no-pager.

I even have this in my `GEMINI.md` in the "priority rules" section:

items.title: refactor(core,cli): emit tool call groups from the scheduler and drop the UI lookahead

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/extensions
labels.description: Issues related to Gemini CLI extensions capability

labels.name: size/l
labels.description: A large sized PR

items.body:
`useGeminiStream` decided on its own which finished tool calls belong together. For sub-agent calls it looked ahead through the live tool list and held a finished call back until every following consecutive agent call had finished too, and it merged consecutive agent calls into one history item by checking the tool kind. A `TODO` in that code asked for `packages/core` to provide those boundaries instead. This change does that: the scheduler marks each run of two or more consecutive sub-agent calls in a batch with a shared `groupId`, and the hook only holds back and merges calls that share a `groupId`. The lookahead and the `Kind.Agent` checks are gone from the hook. For parallel sub-agents the behavior is the same as before.

## Details

- **`ToolCallRequestInfo.groupId` (`packages/core/src/scheduler/types.ts`)**: new optional field. Calls with the same value are presented, and treated as finished, together. The calls of a group are adjacent in their batch. A call that is not part of a group leaves it unset.
- **`Scheduler` (`packages/core/src/scheduler/scheduler.ts`)**:
  - `_startBatch` assigns the groups once per batch, after the requests are ordered, with the new `getToolCallGroupIds` helper. A run of two or more adjacent calls to tools of kind `Kind.Agent` shares the call ID of the first call in the run. A lone agent call and every other call get no group. A tool that is not registered counts as not being an agent.
  - A tail call keeps the group of the call it replaces.
  - The ID is part of the call request, so it is included in every `TOOL_CALLS_UPDATE` snapshot and stays with the call through its status changes. No new event type is needed.
- **`useGeminiStream` (`packages/cli/src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.ts`)**, in the effect that pushes finished tools to history:
  - A finished call that has a `groupId` waits until every call with the same `groupId` has finished (success, error or cancelled). Calls ahead of the group are still pushed in order.
  - Calls with the same `groupId` are pushed as one history item. Calls without a `groupId` are pushed one by one as soon as they finish, as before.
  - The lookahead and its `TODO(#22883)` comment are removed, and the hook no longer imports `Kind`.
- **Unchanged behavior**:
  - `ToolGroupMessage` still derives how it draws consecutive agent calls from the tool kind. That also covers restored sessions, which do not go through the scheduler. Moving it to `groupId` would be a follow-up.
  - Execution is untouched: which calls run in parallel is still decided by `isParallelizable`.
  - Sequential agent calls are still grouped, because a group follows the order of the requests in the batch and not how the calls are executed.
- **Tests**:
  - `packages/core/src/scheduler/scheduler_parallel.test.ts`: contiguous agent calls share the ID of the first call; a lone agent call is not grouped; a new group starts after a call that is not an agent; agent calls separated by another call or by an unregistered tool are not grouped; groups are computed after topic updates move to the front.
  - `packages/core/src/scheduler/scheduler.test.ts`: a tail call keeps the group of the call it replaces.
  - `packages/cli/src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.test.tsx`: new `Grouped Tool Calls` tests. A group is held back until all of its calls have finished and is then pushed as one item; failed and cancelled calls count as finished; calls are grouped by `groupId` and not by tool kind; calls without a `groupId` are pushed individually; finished calls ahead of a group that is still running are pushed while the group waits. The old lookahead had no direct test coverage.
  - On the previous code, 4 of the 7 new core tests and 2 of the 5 new hook tests fail. The others pass before and after the change, because they pin behavior that is meant to stay the same.

## Related Issues

Fixes [#28258](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/28258)

## How to Validate

1. Run the targeted unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/scheduler/scheduler_parallel.test.ts src/scheduler/scheduler.test.ts
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.test.tsx
   ```
2. Run the full preflight:
   ```bash
   npm run preflight
   ```
3. Manual check. This is not easy to do by hand: the difference only shows while two or more sub-agents run in the same turn. That needs a real model session, and the model decides what to call and when each agent finishes. The unit tests above cover the logic, so treat this as an optional smoke test:
   1. Build and start the CLI from this branch:
      ```bash
      npm run build
      npm start
      ```
   2. Ask for two sub-agents in one turn. Any two enabled sub-agents work, for example:
      ```
      Run two codebase_investigator tasks in parallel: one on how the scheduler orders tool calls, and one on how finished tool calls are added to the history.
      ```
   3. Expected, and the same as before this change:
      - While the agents run, both stay together in the live tool area.
      - When the last agent finishes, both results move into the history together as one block. An agent that finished earlier is not printed on its own first.
   4. If the model does not call two agents in the same turn, the check does not apply. Try another prompt.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any)

items.title: fix(core): don't anchor nested .gitignore patterns that only have a trailing slash

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/core
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

labels.name: size/s
labels.description: A small PR

items.body:
Fixes #29290

This is the minimal fix I described in that issue on September 11: when deciding whether to anchor a pattern from a nested `.gitignore`, count only the slashes **before the last character**.

```diff
-if (!isAnchoredInFile && !p.includes('/')) {
+if (!isAnchoredInFile && !p.slice(0, -1).includes('/')) {
```

`build/` in `pkg/.gitignore` then becomes `/pkg/**/build/` instead of `/pkg/build/`, which is what gitignore(5) asks for: a trailing slash restricts the pattern to directories, it does not anchor it. Patterns with a leading or middle slash (`/c`, `c/d`, `c/d/`) are anchored exactly as before, and the root `.gitignore` and `.geminiignore` go through another branch that is untouched.

The regression test covers the reported layout — `pkg/build/out.js` and `pkg/tools/build/out.js` with `build/` in `pkg/.gitignore` — plus the anchored patterns, to show they did not move.

I kept this deliberately small: two files, +14 −2. #29323 fixes the same root cause but also adds an `ignorePatternUtils` module, an `isAncestorDirectoryIgnored` check in `FileDiscoveryService` and symlink handling in `getFolderStructure` (+399 −6 across seven files). Those are reasonable ideas, they are just a different and much wider change, and I would rather you be able to take the one-line correctness fix on its own. Happy to close this if you prefer the broader scope.

Verified by running `packages/core` unit tests on Linux: the new test fails on `main` and passes with this change, and the existing `gitIgnoreParser` tests stay green.

AI tools used

items.title: fix(core): treat whitespace-only UTF-16 and UTF-32 files as empty

labels.name: area/core
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

labels.name: size/m
labels.description: A medium sized PR

items.body:
`isEmpty()` removed the byte order mark and then always decoded the sampled bytes as UTF-8. In UTF-16 and UTF-32 a whitespace character is two or four bytes wide, so decoding it as UTF-8 leaves NUL characters behind, and `trim()` does not strip NUL. A file that held only whitespace was therefore reported as non-empty, and `validatePlanContent()` accepted a whitespace-only plan file saved as UTF-16 or UTF-32 with a BOM. This change decodes the sampled bytes according to the detected BOM, the same way `readFileWithEncoding()` already does.

## Details

- **`decodeBOMContent` (`packages/core/src/utils/fileUtils.ts`)**: new helper that skips the BOM and decodes the remaining bytes according to the BOM's encoding (UTF-8, UTF-16 LE/BE, UTF-32 LE/BE). It is the switch that used to live inline at the end of `readFileWithEncoding()`.
- **`isEmpty`**: uses `decodeBOMContent` for files that start with a BOM. Files without a BOM are still decoded as UTF-8.
- **`readFileWithEncoding`**: calls the same helper, so reading a file and checking whether it is empty cannot drift apart again. Its behavior is unchanged.
- **`decodeUTF16BE`**: ignores an incomplete trailing code unit instead of throwing. `Buffer.swap16()` throws on an odd number of bytes. Because `isEmpty` now reaches this decoder, such a file would otherwise fall into the catch-all in `isEmpty` and be reported as empty even though it contains text. This matches how Node's UTF-16 LE decoder and `decodeUTF32` treat an incomplete trailing unit.
- **Unchanged behavior**:
  - Only the first 1 KB of the file is sampled.
  - A file that cannot be read is still treated as empty.
  - Files without a BOM, and UTF-8 files with a BOM, give the same results as before.
- **Tests**:
  - `packages/core/src/utils/fileUtils.test.ts`: for UTF-8, UTF-16 LE/BE and UTF-32 LE/BE files, all with a BOM, a whitespace-only file is empty, a whitespace-only file larger than the 1 KB sample is empty, and a file with text is not empty. One more test covers a UTF-16 BE file with a trailing partial byte and text, which is not empty.
  - `packages/core/src/utils/planUtils.test.ts`: a whitespace-only UTF-16 LE plan returns the `Plan file is empty` error, and a UTF-16 LE plan with content passes validation.
  - The whitespace-only UTF-16 and UTF-32 cases, and the whitespace-only plan case, fail on the previous code.

## Related Issues

Fixes [#29142](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/29142)

## How to Validate

1. Run the targeted unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/fileUtils.test.ts src/utils/planUtils.test.ts
   ```
2. Run the full preflight:
   ```bash
   npm run preflight
   ```
3. Manual check with throwaway files (nothing in your settings or workspace is touched):
   1. Build, then create three files in a temporary directory. `FF FE` and `FE FF` are the UTF-16 LE and BE byte order marks. Two files contain only a space, a line feed and a tab; the third contains `# Plan`:
      ```bash
      npm run build
      dir="$(mktemp -d)"
      printf '\xff\xfe\x20\x00\x0a\x00\x09\x00' > "$dir/utf16le-whitespace.txt"
      printf '\xfe\xff\x00\x20\x00\x0a\x00\x09' > "$dir/utf16be-whitespace.txt"
      { printf '\xff\xfe'; printf '# Plan' | iconv -f UTF-8 -t UTF-16LE; } > "$dir/utf16le-text.txt"
      ```
   2. Run the plan validation on each file, from the repository root:
      ```bash
      node --input-type=module -e "import { validatePlanContent } from '@google/gemini-cli-core'; for (const f of process.argv.slice(1)) console.log(f.split('/').pop(), '=>', await validatePlanContent(f));" "$dir/utf16le-whitespace.txt" "$dir/utf16be-whitespace.txt" "$dir/utf16le-text.txt"
      ```
      - Expected:
        ```
        utf16le-whitespace.txt => Plan file is empty. You must write content to the plan file before requesting approval.
        utf16be-whitespace.txt => Plan file is empty. You must write content to the plan file before requesting approval.
        utf16le-text.txt => null
        ```
      - Before this change, the two whitespace-only files were accepted (`null`). This is what the new unit tests show on the previous code.
   3. Clean up:
      ```bash
      rm -rf "$dir"
      unset dir
      ```
   - The interactive plan mode flow writes UTF-8 plan files, so it does not produce these inputs on its own. The check above calls the same validation function directly.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any)
- [x] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [ ] MacOS
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
    - [ ] Podman
    - [ ] Seatbelt
  - [ ] Windows
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
  - [x] Linux

items.title: fix(core): vet the permissions of policy directories found by convention

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/enterprise
labels.description: Issues related to Telemetry, Policy, Quota / Licensing

labels.name: size/m
labels.description: A medium sized PR

items.body:
## Summary

`filterSecurePolicyDirectories` ran `isDirectorySecure` on the system policy directory and on nothing else. The user directory and the workspace one are read because that is where the CLI looks, not because anyone named them — so their permissions are the only thing vouching for them, and nothing checked those.

## Details

The docstring already draws the right line, it was just drawn in the wrong place:

> Supplemental admin policy paths are NOT subject to strict security checks as they are explicitly provided by the user/administrator via flags or settings.

That reasoning holds for `adminPolicyPaths` and for `policyPaths` in settings: someone typed those, and vetting them would second-guess a deliberate choice. It does not hold for `Storage.getUserPoliciesDir()` or `settings.workspacePoliciesDir`, which `getPolicyDirectories` adds on its own.

So the filter now takes the **set of directories to check** rather than one special-cased path. A directory found by convention is in it; a path someone named is not, which is what keeps it exempt — no special case threaded through the filter, and the exemption is visible where the set is built.

An insecure directory is skipped with the same warning the system tier already emitted, now worded for whichever tier it was.

**One thing deliberately left alone:** the issue also suggests a `policyIntegrity` check for the workspace tier and logging which tier each policy came from. Both are additions rather than a hole to close, and the tier is already computed (`getPolicyTier`), so that is a separate change with its own reasoning.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29311

## How to Validate

```
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/policy/config.test.ts
```

38 cells, all green; 4 are new. The whole `src/policy` directory: **377 passed across 15 files**. `npm run typecheck`, `eslint` and `prettier --check` are clean.

**Against `main`, with the new cells in place, 2 fail** — the two that describe the hole:

```
× should filter out an insecure user policy directory it found itself
× should filter out an insecure workspace policy directory
```

The other two new cells pass on `main` too, by design: they pin the exemptions that must *not* change (`policyPaths` named by the user, and a secure workspace directory still loading).

**Each cell was checked against a mutant that breaks the thing it names.** Baseline 38/38 green, source restored and re-verified; every mutation asserts it changed the file first:

| mutation | result |
| --- | --- |
| check the system directory only (the behaviour on `main`) | **2 failed** / 36 passed |
| check every directory, named ones included | **2 failed** / 36 passed |
| check nothing | **3 failed** / 35 passed |
| keep an insecure directory instead of dropping it | **3 failed** / 35 passed |
| stop vetting the user directory | **1 failed** / 37 passed |
| *(restored)* | **38 passed** |

The second row is why two of the new cells assert an exemption rather than a rejection: hardening everything would be the easy over-correction, and it would break the choice the docstring deliberately protects.

An earlier version of this change guarded the user directory with `if (!settings.policyPaths?.length)`. The battery showed that mutation surviving, and it was right to: `getPolicyDirectories` uses `policyPaths` *instead of* the default user directory, never both, so the guard could not fire. It is gone rather than kept as a branch nothing reaches.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [ ] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any) <!-- a world-writable user or workspace policy directory is now skipped with a warning instead of loaded -->
- [ ] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [x] MacOS
    - [x] npm run

items.title: fix(vscode-ide-companion): resolve stop() with an MCP stream open

labels.name: area/core
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

labels.name: size/m
labels.description: A medium sized PR

items.body:
Fixes #28785.

`IdeServer.stop()` awaits `this.server.close()`. That callback fires only once every established connection has drained, and the MCP transport holds a long-lived streaming response on `GET /mcp`, so nothing drains. `stop()` never resolves and extension deactivate blocks behind it. VS Code then reports the extension as unresponsive on shutdown.

## What changed

`stop()` now clears the keep-alive intervals, closes the open transports, and calls `closeAllConnections()` alongside `close()`. Closing the transports is what lets the stream drain; `closeAllConnections()` releases anything still holding a socket.

Keep-alive intervals are tracked in a `Set` that is written immediately after `setInterval` returns, not in `onsessioninitialized`. A transport whose handshake never completes is in neither `transports` nor any session map, so an interval registered at initialization time would leave that timer running against a server that is already gone.

The `missedPings >= 3` branch has always logged `Closing connection and cleaning up interval`, but only cleared the interval. It now closes the transport too, which is what the message says and what drops the session.

## What I did not change

The `missedPings = 0` reset on success. The issue I filed lists it, and on reflection consecutive-miss counting is a reasonable reading of "missed pings" rather than a bug. Changing the threshold semantics is a policy call, it is what took the previous attempt at this out of scope, and the leak it was worried about is closed by `stop()` clearing every interval regardless.

## On the test, and what it does not prove

The raw mechanism does reproduce on this Node. A plain server holding one streaming response, then `close()`:

```
stream open; calling server.close()
close callback NEVER fired -> bug reproduces on node v24.10.0
```

The added test opens a real session, holds a real `GET /mcp` stream, and asserts `stop()` resolves. Being straight about it: that assertion alone passes with or without this change in the vitest harness, so on its own it is a regression guard, not a reproduction.

What makes it fail-first is the second assertion, that `stop()` logs `Session closed: <id>`. That only happens if `stop()` actually closes the transport, and `onclose` is what clears the keep-alive interval and drops the session. Reverting `stop()` to its previous body and keeping the test fails on exactly that line. An idle socket does not reproduce anything either, since `close()` destroys those, which is why the test does the full handshake.

## Gates

`npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` clean. `vitest run src/` in `packages/vscode-ide-companion`: 41 passed, 1 skipped.

Two files, no API changes.

items.title: fix(core): pass resumed session data through config init to avoid orphan session file

labels.name: size/m
labels.description: A medium sized PR

items.body:
## The bug

`gemini --resume <uuid>` reuses the resumed session's id for the process
(`resolveSessionId` returns `sessionData.sessionId`). But `config.initialize()`
starts the Gemini client with **no** resumed session data:

```ts
await this._geminiClient.initialize();
```

`GeminiClient.initialize()` → `GeminiChat.initialize(undefined)` then takes the
"create new session" branch in `ChatRecordingService`, opening a **second**
JSONL file:

```
session-<UTC minute>-<session id[0:8]>.jsonl
```

Because the process id is the resumed session's real id, this orphan file
carries the *same* eight-character suffix as the real conversation file, and
holds nothing but an initial metadata line — the recorder never uses it, since
`useSessionResume`'s `resumeChat()` call (which does receive the resumed data
and correctly reopens the real file) only runs later, in a React effect.

That empty orphan is never cleaned up on its own exit path, either — cleanup
only runs against `config.getGeminiClient().getChatRecordingService()`, which
after `resumeChat()` completes points at the *real* file, not the orphan.
The orphan is what a later startup's session-retention sweep finds:
`hasResumableContent` is false for it, so it is treated as corrupted, and
cleanup derives the short id from its filename and expands the deletion to
*every* file ending in that same `-<shortId>.jsonl` — including the real
conversation. That's exactly what's reported in #29198: after resuming a
session and exiting without interacting, trying to resume the same session
again later shows it gone from `--list-sessions` and `--resume <uuid>` fails.

## The fix

Thread `resumedSessionData` through the one call site that was dropping it:

```
config.initialize(resumedSessionData)
  -> GeminiClient.initialize(resumedSessionData)
    -> startChat(undefined, resumedSessionData)
      -> GeminiChat.initialize(resumedSessionData)
        -> ChatRecordingService reopens the existing file instead of creating a new one
```

- `packages/core/src/config/config.ts`: `initialize()`/`_initialize()` accept
  and forward `resumedSessionData` to `this._geminiClient.initialize(...)`.
- `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`: `GeminiClient.initialize()` accepts
  `resumedSessionData` and passes it to `startChat()`.
- `packages/cli/src/gemini.tsx` and `packages/cli/src/ui/AppContainer.tsx`:
  the two call sites of `config.initialize()` (non-interactive and interactive
  paths) now pass the `resumedSessionData` they already have in scope.

History is untouched by this change — `startChat(undefined, resumedSessionData)`
still passes no `extraHistory`, so the in-memory chat history continues to be
built exclusively by the later `resumeChat()` call in `useSessionResume`. This
change only fixes which file chat recording targets from the start.

## Test plan

Added a regression test in `packages/core/src/core/client.test.ts` asserting
that `GeminiClient.initialize(resumedSessionData)` forwards the data to
`startChat`. Verified it fails without the fix:

```
$ git checkout HEAD~1 -- packages/core/src/core/client.ts
$ npm test --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/core/client.test.ts -t initialize
 FAIL  src/core/client.test.ts > Gemini Client (client.ts) > initialize > passes resumed session data to startChat so recording reopens the existing file
 AssertionError: expected "startChat" to be called with arguments: [ undefined, …(1) ]
 Received: [[]]  (called with no resumedSessionData)
$ git checkout HEAD -- packages/core/src/core/client.ts
```

With the fix, the full targeted suites pass:

```
$ npm test --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/core/client.test.ts src/config/config.test.ts src/services/chatRecordingService.test.ts src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
 Test Files  4 passed (4)
      Tests  480 passed | 1 skipped (481)

$ npm test --workspace @google/gemini-cli -- src/ui/AppContainer.test.tsx
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  112 passed (112)
```

`src/gemini.test.tsx` has 9 pre-existing failures (`FatalUntrustedWorkspaceError:
Gemini CLI is not running in a trusted directory`) that reproduce identically
on unmodified `main` in this sandbox — unrelated to this change (headless/CI
trusted-folder detection in the test environment).

`npx eslint` and `npx prettier --check` are clean on all changed files, and
`npm run typecheck` passes across all workspaces.

Fixes #29198.

---

_This PR was prepared with AI assistance (an autonomous coding agent
investigated the issue, traced the root cause, wrote the fix, and verified it
with the tests above). A human reviewed the change before submission._

items.title: fix(core): let /ide enable reconnect after the IDE server restarts

labels.name: area/core
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

labels.name: size/l
labels.description: A large sized PR

labels.name: size/xl
labels.description: An extra large PR

items.body:
## Summary

After VS Code's **Developer: Reload Window** (or an extension update/disable), the CLI running in the surviving integrated terminal reported `🔴 Disconnected: IDE connection error…`, and `/ide enable` kept failing with `Failed to connect to IDE companion extension…` until VS Code was fully closed and reopened.

#29674 fixed the server side of #28785 (`IdeServer.stop()` hanging and leaking its port file). This PR fixes the **client side**, which could not survive an IDE-server restart even with a fixed extension — and still cannot with the Marketplace extension (v0.20.0), which predates #29674 and leaks a port file on every reload.

Two defects in `IdeClient`:

1. **Discovery tried a single port file.** The reloaded extension host starts a new server (new port, new token, new port file), but the terminal's `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_PORT` / `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_AUTH_TOKEN` stay frozen at the old values. `getConnectionConfigFromFile()` used that frozen port as the tie-breaker, so a leaked old file was selected deterministically, `connect()` never fell through to the live file, and the env fallback pointed at the same dead port.
2. **A superseded client kept driving the state.** `onerror`/`onclose` were bound to the `IdeClient`, not to the client that registered them, and `establish*Connection()` never closed the previous client. After a successful `/ide enable`, the old transport's SSE reconnection attempts against the dead port (1 s, 2.5 s) flipped the state back to `Disconnected` while the new connection was healthy.

Two source files in `packages/core`, no public API change, no new `eslint-disable`.

## Details

### `ide-connection-utils.ts`

- New `getConnectionConfigsFromFile(pid)` returns **every** workspace-valid candidate, best first: the file whose port matches `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_PORT` (the window the terminal belongs to), then the rest in the existing `sortConnectionFiles()` order. When no file matches the workspace it still returns the single best-sorted entry so the detailed "Directory mismatch" error is preserved.
- `getConnectionConfigFromFile()` is now `candidates[0]` — the ranking of the preferred file is **unchanged** (all 46 pre-existing tests pass untouched). The three inline config types were replaced by an exported `IdeConnectionConfig` alias. The module is not re-exported from core's index.

### `ide-client.ts`

- `connect()` iterates the candidates, each with **its own** auth token, before the env fallbacks. Behaviour is identical whenever the first candidate answers — the only case that worked before.
- `registerClientHandlers()` captures the client it is registering for; `onerror`/`onclose` no-op once `this.client` has moved on.
- New `retireClient()`, called by both `establishHttpConnection()` and `establishStdioConnection()` before creating a new `Client`: detaches the handlers and `close()`s the superseded client (aborting its socket and retry timers); a rejected `close()` is debug-logged.
- A failed attempt no longer leaves `this.client` pointing at a `Client` that never connected (`dropFailedClient()`, scoped to that attempt's client), so `openDiff`/`closeDiff` fail fast on `!this.client`; failed attempts are debug-logged. (Review feedback.)

### Deliberately out of scope

- Deleting stale files from the client (unsafe when the CLI runs in a sandbox/remote where a port is legitimately unreachable); an extension-side GC of dead sibling files is a natural follow-up.
- Auto-reconnect on disconnect (policy change). Users still see one `IDE connection error… run /ide enable` line after a reload; this PR makes that documented recovery actually work.
- Carried over: a stale file whose port was reused by an unrelated process that accepts TCP but never answers would wait for the SDK's `initialize` timeout (same exposure as before, now per candidate).

## Related Issues

Related to #28785 — client-side follow-up to #29674 (which fixed `IdeServer.stop()`; the issue was closed by it, but the reload symptom it mentions remained).

## How to Validate

**Unit / integration tests**

```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/ide/
# 7 files, 185 passed | 1 skipped
```

- `ide-connection-utils.test.ts` — +9 cases for `getConnectionConfigsFromFile` (legacy file, empty/error paths, workspace filtering and order, env-port promotion with fallbacks retained, no env match, mismatch → single entry, malformed files, singular returns the first candidate).
- `ide-client.test.ts` — +13 cases: candidate iteration (next candidate on failure with its own token, stop at first success, http → stdio candidate, env fallback after all candidates, disconnected when nothing answers), reconnecting (superseded client closed and detached, its late error/close ignored, errors from the current client still reported, rejected `close()` tolerated) and failed attempts (HTTP and stdio failures leave no client behind, `openDiff`/`closeDiff` fail fast, a later successful candidate's client is kept). Also fixes the latent singleton reset in that file (`instancePromise`, not `instance`) so its tests are actually isolated.
- `ide-client.server-restart.test.ts` (new) — real `node:http` MCP servers and real port files in a private `TMPDIR`, no SDK mocks: (1) leaked file matching the frozen env port, (2) late errors from the superseded transport after a clean restart, (3) several leaked files with no env hint, (4) the env-matching window still wins when several servers are alive. (1) and (2) fail on `main` with exactly the user-facing messages above and pass with this change.

**End-to-end with the real `/ide` commands** (harness kept out of the tree): the real `ideCommand()` actions from `packages/cli`, the real `IdeClient`, and the real companion `IDEServer` (vscode API mocked), executed as stash-fix → rebuild → run → restore → rebuild → run:

| Step | `main` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/ide status` | `🟢 Connected` | `🟢 Connected` |
| Reload Window (A: v0.20.0 leaks file · B: fixed extension) | — | — |
| `/ide status` ≈1 s later | `🔴 Disconnected: IDE connection error…` | same (by design, one notification) |
| `/ide enable` | A: `🔴 Disconnected: Failed to connect to IDE companion extension…`  | `🟢 Connected` |
| `/ide status` 4.5 s later | B: `🔴 Disconnected: IDE connection error…` | `🟢 Connected`, `isDiffingEnabled() === true` |

**Manually in VS Code**

1. `rm -f /tmp/gemini/ide/gemini-ide-server-*.json` (macOS: `$TMPDIR/gemini/ide/`), open the repo, run `gemini` in the integrated terminal, `/ide status` → `🟢 Connected to VS Code`.
2. **Developer: Reload Window**; keep the terminal. Within ~1–2 s the CLI prints `IDE connection error… run /ide enable`.
3. `/ide enable` → **before:** `🔴 Disconnected: Failed to connect to IDE companion extension in VS Code…` (with the Marketplace extension; `ls /tmp/gemini/ide/` shows the leaked old file next to the new one) — **after:** `🟢 Connected to VS Code`, and `/ide status` stays connected; diffs work.

**CI parity (Linux, Node 20.20.2):** all `ci.yml` Lint-job steps (lockfile, eslint, actionlint, shellcheck, yamllint, build, typecheck, prettier, settings docs `--check`, sensitive keywords, actions pinning) and both Test (Linux) shards + `test:scripts` + bundle + bundle/npx smoke tests ran locally and passed; `npm run preflight` passed (cli 7327, core 8341, a2a 177, companion 62, scripts 202 tests).

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed) — not needed: docs already tell users to run `/ide enable` to reconnect and tell plugin authors to delete their discovery file on deactivation; this change makes that recovery work.
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any) — none
- [ ] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [ ] MacOS
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
    - [ ] Podman
    - [ ] Seatbelt
  - [ ] Windows
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
  - [x] Linux
    - [x] npm run
    - [x] npx
    - [ ] Docker

items.title: fix(acp): don't start a fresh chat before resuming, it poisons the session file

labels.name: priority/p1
labels.description: Important and should be addressed in the near term.

labels.name: area/core
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

labels.name: size/m
labels.description: A medium sized PR

items.body:
Partially addresses #28693 — see the correction below; this removes one of two fresh-chat starts on the load path, not both.

> **Correction (2026-08-10).** `loadSession` calls `initializeSessionConfig` first, and that ends with `await config.initialize()`, which itself calls `this._geminiClient.initialize()`. So there were **two** fresh-chat starts ahead of `resumeChat`, and this PR only removes the second. The test here could not catch that because `mockConfig.initialize` is a stub. #28767 fixes the underlying cause by handing the resumed session data to `config.initialize()`; the remaining ACP work after that is to resolve the session before `initializeSessionConfig` and pass it through. The removal in this PR is still correct on its own merits — `resumeChat` already does everything `initialize()` does — but it does not close #28693 by itself.

## Problem

`loadSession` called `geminiClient.initialize()` immediately before `resumeChat()`:

```ts
const geminiClient = config.getGeminiClient();
await geminiClient.initialize();          // starts a chat with NO resumed session data
await geminiClient.resumeChat(clientHistory, { conversation: sessionData, filePath: sessionPath });
```

`initialize()` is `this.chat = await this.startChat()` with no `resumedSessionData`, so `ChatRecordingService.initialize(undefined)` takes the fresh-conversation branch and writes a metadata header plus a `$set` checkpoint.

The recording filename is keyed on the UTC minute and the session id prefix — `session-<UTC-minute>-<id[0:8]>.jsonl` (`chatRecordingService.ts:495-519`). So when the load happens **in the same UTC minute the session was created**, that append lands in the session's own conversation file. The checkpoint buries the conversation in the fold, `hasResumableContent` flips false, the session is filtered out of the listing, and the load fails with `No previous sessions found for this project` — after durably destroying the session's resumability, so every later load for that id fails too.

No crash is required; it reproduces after a clean exit. Automated clients that reconnect immediately land in this window, while a human retrying minutes later lands in a different minute and sees loads succeed — which is why it read as intermittent or environment-dependent.

Credit to @realtonyyoung for the repro and for re-root-causing it; I'd earlier ruled out four candidate mechanisms on the issue and the load path was what was left.

## Approach

Remove the `initialize()` call. `resumeChat` already does everything it does — it sets `this.chat` via `startChat(history, resumedSessionData)` and calls `updateTelemetryTokenCount()` — so the call was redundant as well as destructive. One line out, plus a comment recording why it must not come back.

This deliberately does **not** change the filename scheme. Minute-precision plus an 8-char id prefix is a real collision surface, but widening it would change where existing sessions are looked up, and it isn't needed here: nothing should be writing a fresh-conversation header during a load in the first place.

## How tested

- `resumes without first starting a fresh chat for the same session id` asserts the client is resumed directly with the resolved session data and never initialized for a fresh chat. It fails on the parent commit with `expected "spy" to not be called at all, but actually been called 1 times`.
- Full ACP suite: **92 passed across 10 files**.
- `eslint --max-warnings 0` and `prettier --check` clean; `npm run typecheck` exit 0. The repo's `pre-commit` hook ran clean on the staged files.

Developed with Claude Code; reviewed and tested by Pranav before marking ready for review.

items.title: fix(cli): --resume opens a second session file, and cleanup deletes the real one

labels.name: priority/p1
labels.description: Important and should be addressed in the near term.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: size/m
labels.description: A medium sized PR

items.body:
## The bug

`gemini --resume` reuses the resumed session's id for the process ([`resolveSessionId`](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/cli/src/gemini.tsx#L306-L313) returns `sessionData.sessionId`), and then `config.initialize()` starts a chat with **no** resumed session data. `ChatRecordingService.initialize(undefined)` takes the "create new session" branch and opens a second file:

```
session-<UTC minute>-<session id[0:8]>.jsonl
```

The resumed conversation keeps going into its original file, so this new one never holds anything but a metadata header.

That empty file is the collision generator behind #27368 and #27877. Reporters described the intermediate state precisely before anyone had a root cause — one extra JSONL per resume, same eight-character suffix, new timestamp, only initial metadata, "effectively unused" ([#27368](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/27368#issuecomment-5081412297), and eight such files for one session id in [#27877](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/27877)).

The loss happens on the next launch:

1. `getAllSessionFiles` returns the orphan with `sessionInfo: null`, because `hasResumableContent` is false.
2. `identifySessionsToDelete` treats every `sessionInfo === null` entry as corrupted and schedules it for deletion.
3. [`cleanupExpiredSessions`](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/cli/src/utils/sessionCleanup.ts#L152-L167) derives the short id from the doomed filename and expands it to *every* file ending in `-<shortId>.jsonl` — which includes the real conversation.
4. The only guard is `fullSessionId !== config.getSessionId()`, and on a normal launch the current session id is a fresh uuid, so it does not protect the previous session.

The session is gone from `/chat`, permanently, which is what @suiryc reported: the target session is wiped "the next time you use the CLI to start a new session or even simply list available sessions."

## The fix

`config.initialize()` takes the resumed session data and hands it to `GeminiClient.initialize()`, which forwards it to `startChat` so chat recording reopens the existing file instead of creating a second one.

History is deliberately untouched here — only the recording target changes. `startChat(undefined, resumedSessionData)` passes no `extraHistory`, so the model context is still built exclusively by `resumeChat` later in `useSessionResume`. There is no double-replay.

It also closes a smaller loss on the same path: quitting a `--resume` before the UI finishes resuming ran `deleteCurrentSessionIfNotResumableAsync` against the empty file, and that helper deletes artifacts by *full* session id — the resumed session's logs and tool-output directory. With recording pointed at the real file from the start, the resumable check sees the real conversation and leaves everything alone.

## What this does not touch

- **The cleanup expansion itself.** #28653 already narrows retention cleanup to the files it actually selected, and that is worth having independently: an eight-character suffix can collide on its own. This PR removes the thing that manufactures collisions on every resume; that one stops a collision from being fatal. They are complementary, and neither makes the other redundant.
- **The filename scheme.** Minute precision plus eight characters is a real collision surface, but widening it changes where existing sessions are found and it is not what breaks here.
- **ACP `session/load`.** Same class of defect, separate entry point — see the note below.

## A correction on #28744

While tracing this I found that my own PR #28744 is necessary but not sufficient. It removes the redundant `geminiClient.initialize()` in `AcpSessionManager.loadSession`, but `initializeSessionConfig` calls `config.initialize()` first, and that reaches `_geminiClient.initialize()` too. The test there mocks `config.initialize`, so it could not see the second source. I have said so on that PR. This change is what actually closes that path, once ACP resolves its session before initializing config; happy to do that as a follow-up.

## Verification

All three regression tests fail on the parent commit and pass here:

| test | failure on `eef19f2` |
| --- | --- |
| `config.test.ts` › hands resumed session data to the Gemini client | `expected "spy" to be called with arguments: [ { conversation: …, filePath: … } ]` |
| `client.test.ts` › passes resumed session data to startChat | `expected "spy" to be called with arguments: [ undefined, …(1) ]` |
| `AppContainer.test.tsx` › tells config a resume is in flight | `expected "initialize" to be called with arguments: [ { conversation: …, filePath: … } ]` |

A fourth test in `chatRecordingService.test.ts` locks the invariant the plumbing depends on: initializing with resumed data reopens the existing file and leaves the chats directory with exactly one entry.

```bash
npx vitest run --root packages/core src/core/client.test.ts src/config/config.test.ts src/services/chatRecordingService.test.ts src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
npx vitest run --root packages/cli src/ui/AppContainer.test.tsx src/utils/sessionCleanup.test.ts src/utils/sessionUtils.test.ts src/acp
npm run typecheck
```

- Targeted suites: **467 passed** (core), **310 passed across 14 files** (cli).
- Full suites: core **7784 passed**, cli **6949 passed**. The 6 core and 9 cli failures on my machine (`sandboxManager.integration`, `modelConfig.golden`, `topic-policy`, `gemini.test.tsx` trusted-folder) reproduce identically on pristine `main` — environment, not this change.
- `eslint --max-warnings 0` clean, `prettier --check` clean, `npm run typecheck` exit 0, pre-commit hook clean.

Fixes #27368.
Fixes #27877.

items.title: Edit tool: flexible match drops newline

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

items.body:
### What happened?

The edit tool seems to be removing a newline when it has to fall back to fuzzy/flexible matching

So if my file has:

  hello
    world
  end

and the model tries to replace hello\nworld with goodbye\nmoon, I end up with:

  goodbye
  moon  end

moon and end just get mushed together on the same line instead of maintaining them on separate lines

### What did you expect to happen?

end should still be on its own line after the replacement. The rest of the file shouldn't be affected.

### Client information

on windows

### Login information

Google Account (Standard CLI Login)

### Anything else we need to know?

This only seems to happen when flexible matching kicks in (i.e. when there's an indentation mismatch between old_string and what's actually in the file). If the exact match succeeds, the output is fine.
